Palm Springs, California · ride

Bike routes in Palm Springs

The rides locals in Palm Springs actually do, each with a public route page you can load on your computer. Real miles, real feet, where it starts, where the water is, and the line about what will get you hurt.

Best months: October to April. The Tour de Palm Springs FAQ puts February highs at 60 to 70 and lows at 50 to 55. PJAMM puts June-to-September highs at the foot of Highway 74 at 102 to 108 F and says not to start after sunrise then; Velo Palm Springs gives Joshua Tree a riding window of roughly October to April. The Desert Bicycle Club's weekend rides are on its calendar from October, and Big Wheel Bikes' Palm Springs store closes for the summer.

Bike routes in Palm Springs, listed

  1. CV Link, West Valley (Palm Springs to Cathedral City)

    Path · 20 mi · easy · Wide paved path, with a decomposed-granite walking and running path beside it on most of it. The Palm Desert piece switches between path and street.

    Route page

    Zone 2, the valley floor, and the ride for the day you land. The valley's car-free path: about 40 miles in three pieces, finished in 2025. The Palm Springs piece runs 19.63 miles from the Palm Springs Visitor Center, along the Chino Wash and the Whitewater River levee, to Date Palm Drive in Cathedral City. A spur follows Tahquitz Creek through Demuth Park. Join it anywhere and turn around anywhere; there's an access point with street parking at Via Escuela and Executive Drive, just east of Gene Autry Trail. CVAG posts no hours, and solar lights set in the path mark it at night. The other two pieces are in Palm Desert (5.44 miles, Bump and Grind trailhead to Cook Street) and from La Quinta to Coachella (16.02 miles, Washington Street to Airport Boulevard). The west end is the foot of Tramway Road, so the two make one day: flat miles out, the wall on the way back.

    Start: Palm Springs Visitor Center, Highway 111 at Tramway Road (the west end)

    Water: Hydration stations at the rest stops. Patch counted 30 rest stops with benches, bike racks and hydration stations (Sept 2026). CVAG lists restrooms at the Palm Springs Visitor Center, Esperanza Park, the Bump and Grind access point, Palm Desert Civic Park, North Jackson Park and Sierra Vista Park.

    Watch: You share it with e-bikes, electric scooters and golf carts. The limit is 20 mph for bikes and carts and 15 for scooters (CVAG). It isn't one path end to end. Rancho Mirage and Indian Wells pulled out of the project, so the path stops at their city lines (Palm Springs Post, Nov 2025): the West Valley piece ends at Date Palm Drive, and the next piece starts in Palm Desert. In November 2025 Palm Springs listed work under way at the Sunrise Way undercrossing and along the Tahquitz Creek corridor. Check the CVAG map before a long ride. Wind can come up at any time. Heat: in the hot months, roughly May to October, ride early or late (Coachella Valley Independent, April 2026); PJAMM puts June-to-September highs in Palm Desert at 102 to 108 F.

  2. Tramway Road

    Climb · 4 mi · 1,900 ft · hard · Paved road; a separated paved path runs beside it on the south side.

    RideWithGPSRoute page

    Zone 1, the climb you can ride to from a downtown hotel. Tramway Road from Highway 111 up toward the Palm Springs Aerial Tramway's valley station: 3.8 miles and 1,918 feet at 9.5 percent average (PJAMM), steepening all the way; myCols puts the max at 13.9 percent and Palm Springs Life says the last quarter mile touches 19. The 2013 Tour of California finished Stage 2 here. It starts where CV Link starts, so it pairs with the path: flat miles out, the wall on the way back. RideWithGPS 11063650 is an 18.5-mile loop from downtown that climbs it. The tram car itself is under Off the bike.

    Start: Tramway Road at Highway 111 (the Palm Springs Visitor Center, the west end of CV Link)

    Water: CVAG lists restrooms at the Palm Springs Visitor Center at the foot (see the CV Link entry). Nothing on the climb is named on any page fetched.

    Watch: Bikes stop at the tramway's toll gate, about half a mile below the parking lot (Palm Springs Life, 2024; riders on PJAMM and myCols say the same, since about 2014), so the posted 3.8 miles is to a line you can't ride to. The top is 19 percent. Heat: in the hot months, roughly May to October, ride early or late (Coachella Valley Independent, April 2026); PJAMM puts June-to-September highs in the valley at 102 to 108 F, so this one is dawn or not at all.

  3. Highway 74, Palms to Pines (from Palm Desert)

    Climb · 14 mi · 3,700 ft · hard · Paved two-lane state highway, in good condition, with little or no shoulder after the first few miles.

    Route page

    Zone 3, the valley's big climb. Highway 74 south out of Palm Desert, 13.9 miles and 3,677 feet at 5.1 percent average, with the steepest quarter mile at 8.3 percent (PJAMM). The road leaves the desert floor, enters the national forest around mile 3.6, and stacks hairpins from mile 4.5 to 8; the Coachella Valley Vista Point at mile 8.4 looks down on all of them. The grade eases near 4,000 feet at the PJAMM finish. Turn there, or keep going toward Pinyon and Idyllwild (Bikemap's 27-mile route to the top of the pass climbs about 4,800 feet). The Desert Bicycle Club's Sunday Climbers (Sundays, 7:30 am) ride it from the Starbucks at your own pace, regrouping at the Art Smith Trailhead (mile 4) and the Vista Point. From downtown Palm Springs the foot of the climb is about 12 miles down the valley.

    Start: Starbucks at Highway 74 and El Paseo, Palm Desert (the foot of the climb), 73030 El Paseo, Palm Desert, CA 92260

    Watch: No to minimal shoulder, and traffic at highway speed both ways; PJAMM calls it 'not a ride for the traffic averse cyclist', and one rider there (April 2023) turned around for it. The club's own warning: past mile 4 the road is narrow and winding with no bike lane. Riders descend at 35 to 40 mph with cars passing at 65. No water, store or restroom on the climb is named on any page fetched; the Vista Point is a 16-car lot. Heat: June-to-September highs run 102 to 108 F, and PJAMM says don't start after sunrise then; in the hot months, roughly May to October, this is a dawn ride.

    Ride it with the group: Desert Bicycle Club Sunday Climbers (Sundays, 7:30 am) →

  4. Tour de Palm Springs century

    Road · 101 mi · 3,150 ft · epic · Paved road and path. The organizer says the 2027 routes use CV Link where they can.

    RideWithGPSRoute page

    Zones 1 and 2, the long one, and Robert's ride. The long route of the Tour de Palm Springs, the valley's big charity ride. It starts and finishes downtown on South Palm Canyon at Tahquitz. The 2027 ride is Saturday, February 6, with routes from 16 to 101 miles; the organizer says the full 2027 maps are coming. A RideWithGPS route of it is 101.4 miles and 3,161 feet; Velo Palm Springs' write-up of an earlier century runs out to Thermal and back. The century rolls at 6:30 a.m.; packet pickup is Friday noon to 8 and Saturday from 6 at South Palm Canyon and Baristo (the Tour's FAQ, Oct 2026). Koffi Palm Springs Central on Tahquitz Canyon Way opens at 6:30 (see Coffee).

    Start: South Palm Canyon Dr at Tahquitz, downtown Palm Springs

    Water: On event day, 3 lunch stops, 2 snack stops and 4 water stops along the routes (organizer). Nothing published for riding it on another day.

    Watch: The organizer says routes and departures can be changed by the host cities, and the 2027 maps weren't out on Oct 3, 2026, so the RideWithGPS line may not be this year's course. On any other day these are open roads with no support; Highway 111, the valley's spine, is its fast road (see Bring your bike). You need the helmet sticker to get into a SAG stop (the Tour's FAQ). Heat: February highs run 60 to 70 (the Tour's FAQ); in the hot months, roughly May to October, PJAMM puts June-to-September highs in Palm Desert at 102 to 108 F, so riding this course out of season is a dawn start.

  5. The Midcentury Modern loop (downtown Palm Springs)

    Road · 8 mi · easy · Paved city streets.

    Route page

    Zone 1, the downtown easy ride. Velo Palm Springs' loop: 7.86 miles, mostly flat with one short climb. It passes eight landmark buildings, among them the Del Marcos Hotel, Albert Frey's Fire Station No. 1 and Frey House II, Sinatra's Twin Palms and the Kaufmann Desert House. The route uses Palm Canyon Drive, Baristo Road, Indian Canyon Drive, Palisades Drive, Alejo Road, Ladera Circle, Hermosa Place and Vista Chino. Do it the evening you land or on a slow morning. It starts at the Architecture and Design Center (see Off the bike), a block south of the Tour start. Street parking on Palm Canyon is metered, and the Civic Center has a parking structure.

    Start: Palm Springs Art Museum Architecture and Design Center, 300 S Palm Canyon Dr, Palm Springs, CA

    Watch: Palm Canyon Drive carries traffic. Velo Palm Springs says to ride it early, when it's cooler and there's less traffic on Palm Canyon. Heat: in the hot months, roughly May to October, ride early or late (Coachella Valley Independent, April 2026); PJAMM puts June-to-September highs in the valley at 102 to 108 F.

  6. Gerald Ford, Tamarisk and Country Club loop (Palm Desert and Rancho Mirage)

    Road · 14 mi · easy · Bike lanes and residential streets, with a stretch on the Abrams-Butler trail.

    Route page

    Zone 2, the way to ride Palm Desert and Rancho Mirage, where CV Link has its gap. A loop of 14-plus miles from Tri-A-Bike's door, from the shop's own list of local rides. It takes San Pablo, Magnesia Falls, Portola, Gerald Ford, Tamarisk, Frank Sinatra, the Abrams-Butler trail and Country Club, among others. Rancho Mirage isn't on CV Link, so this is how you cross it. The shop calls it easy, with a moderate uphill on Portola and on Gerald Ford to Monterey, and lists Trojan Plaza as a second start. The shop's weekly fun ride (Saturdays, 10:30 am) leaves from the same door, any bike.

    Start: Tri-A-Bike, Palm Desert, 44841 San Pablo Ave, Palm Desert, CA 92260

    Watch: The shop's page names only the uphill on Portola and Gerald Ford, and says nothing about traffic on the rest. Heat: in the hot months, roughly May to October, ride early or late (Coachella Valley Independent, April 2026); PJAMM puts June-to-September highs in Palm Desert at 102 to 108 F.

  7. Box Canyon from Mecca

    Road · 20 mi · 1,600 ft · moderate

    Route page

    Zone 4, a car day at the east end of the valley. Tri-A-Bike's ride from 66 Ave and Johnson Rd through Box Canyon to Pinto Road at Interstate 10. That's 19.5 miles one way with a shuttle back, or 39 miles if you turn around and ride down. The shop puts the climbing at 1,590 feet.

    Start: 66 Ave and Johnson Rd, near Mecca

    Watch: The shop rates it advanced. It climbs all the way to the turnaround or the shuttle pickup at I-10. The page names no water stop on the route, so carry all you need, and nothing on the page says what the shoulder or the traffic is like. Heat: this is the low, open end of the valley; in the hot months, roughly May to October, ride early or late (Coachella Valley Independent, April 2026); PJAMM puts June-to-September highs in Palm Desert at 102 to 108 F.

  8. Park Boulevard, Joshua Tree National Park

    Road · 25 mi · moderate · Paved park road, mostly without a shoulder.

    Route page

    Zone 4, a car day over the hills to the north. The main road through the Mojave side of the park. It runs roughly 25 miles between the West and North entrances, over moderate rolling hills (Velo Palm Springs, April 2026). Keys View Road, a paved spur, is a climb of roughly five miles from its turnoff on Park Boulevard to the overlook. A rider pays $15 for a seven-day pass (Velo Palm Springs, read Oct 3, 2026). Velo puts the riding window at roughly October to April.

    Start: West Entrance, Joshua Tree National Park

    Water: None on the park's interior roads. Water only at the park entrances and at the Cottonwood, Black Rock and Indian Cove campgrounds (Velo Palm Springs).

    Watch: There are no bike lanes anywhere in the park, and most paved roads have no shoulder. There is no shade. Cell service is unreliable. Heat: summer temperatures regularly pass 100 F and have reached 124 F (Velo Palm Springs), which is why the riding window is October to April. Keys View Road is exposed and the wind can be strong there; descend carefully.

  9. Geology Tour Road, Joshua Tree National Park

    Gravel · 18 mi · moderate · Dirt road. Riders on wider tires handle it well, per Velo Palm Springs; drivers are told to bring a high-clearance vehicle for the lower section.

    Route page

    Zone 4, the dirt ride, on the same car day as Park Boulevard. An 18-mile out-and-back on dirt (not a loop). It drops south from Park Boulevard through some of the park's most interesting geology, per Velo Palm Springs. Bikes are allowed on every paved and dirt road in the park that's open to cars. No valley shop was found renting a gravel bike; the full-suspension rentals in Palm Desert and Palm Springs would do.

    Start: Geology Tour Road at Park Boulevard

    Water: None. Velo Palm Springs says to carry extra water here.

    Watch: It's remote and shadeless, and there's nothing out there if something goes wrong (Velo Palm Springs). Cell service in the park is unreliable. Heat: summer temperatures in the park regularly pass 100 F and have reached 124 F (Velo Palm Springs); ride it in the October-to-April window, early.
